courses.title: English 10
courses.description: A tenth-grade English course organized around world literature and the rhetoric of power, conflict, and freedom, paired with Modern World History. Students read short fiction, Greek and Shakespearean tragedy, Things Fall Apart, Night, Fahrenheit 451, A Doll's House, war poetry and landmark speeches. Every unit weaves close reading, grammar and vocabulary, discussion, and a major written product (narrative, literary analysis, argument, and a multi-source research paper).

standards.RL.9-10.2: Determine a theme of a literary text, analyze its development, and provide an objective summary.

standards.W.9-10.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas clearly and accurately.

standards.W.9-10.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

standards.SL.9-10.2: Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse media or formats, evaluating credibility and accuracy.
standards.SL.9-10.3: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

weeks.topic: Suspense and structure: 'The Most Dangerous Game'

days.title: Course launch & reading survey
days.work: Complete a reading-history survey, set up a reading journal, and write a one-page 'reader autobiography' as a writing baseline.

days.title: Read Connell, part 1
days.work: Read the first half of 'The Most Dangerous Game' and annotate every foreshadowing clue on Ship-Trap Island with sticky notes or margin marks.

days.title: Read Connell, part 2
days.work: Finish the story and chart the rising tension on a plot diagram, quoting one sentence for each stage.

days.title: Grammar: phrases
days.work: Identify prepositional, participial and appositive phrases in ten sentences from the story, then write five sentences imitating Connell's participial openers.

days.title: Summary & discussion
days.work: Write a 150-word objective summary (no opinion) and discuss with a parent: is Rainsford changed by the end? Cite two lines.

weeks.assessment: Objective summary scored for accuracy and no opinion; plot diagram with quoted evidence.

weeks.topic: Unreliable narrators: Poe's 'The Cask of Amontillado'
objectives: Analyze point of view and irony
Use textual evidence to infer motive

days.title: Irony chart
days.work: Build a three-column chart (quote / what it says / what it really means) for six ironic moments, labeling each verbal or dramatic.

days.title: Word study: Latin roots

days.title: Analytical paragraph
days.work: Write a TIQA paragraph (topic, intro to quote, quote, analysis) answering: Is Montresor a reliable narrator? Cite two pieces of evidence.

days.title: Quiz & revise
days.work: Take a short quiz on irony and point of view, then revise the paragraph using teacher feedback on quote integration.

weeks.assessment: Analytical paragraph rubric (claim, evidence, analysis) and irony quiz.

weeks.topic: Time and twist: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' and 'The Necklace'
objectives: Compare situational irony in two stories

days.title: Film comparison

days.title: Compare endings
days.work: Write a 250-word comparison of the twist endings: how does each author plant clues so the surprise feels earned?

days.title: Socratic discussion

weeks.assessment: Comparison response scored on evidence and analysis of structure; discussion participation checklist.

objectives: Write an original short story using suspense techniques

days.title: Draft opening

days.title: Draft middle & end

days.title: Revise & edit

days.title: Read Prologue

days.title: Read Parodos & Scene 1

days.title: Check & reflect

objectives: Track the role of the chorus

days.title: Read Scene 2

days.title: Stichomythia practice
days.work: Perform the rapid line exchange aloud with a partner and explain how the form heightens conflict.

days.title: Ode 2 & figurative language

days.title: Read Scene 3 – Haemon

days.title: Quiz & journal

weeks.topic: Antigone: Downfall and the tragic hero

days.title: Seminar

weeks.topic: Argument essay: Antigone and civil disobedience

days.work: Draft the 700–900 word essay, integrating quotes from both the play and Thoreau.

days.title: Grammar: parallel structure
days.work: Mini-lesson on parallel structure; revise three sentences in your draft to use parallelism for emphasis.

days.title: Final draft & unit test
days.work: Submit the final essay and take the Unit 2 test on tragic conventions and vocabulary.

weeks.topic: Things Fall Apart Part 1: Igbo society

courses.title: Geometry
courses.description: A full-year high school Geometry course following the CA Common Core traditional pathway. Students build geometry from transformations, write two-column, paragraph and coordinate proofs, and apply congruence, similarity, right-triangle trigonometry, circles, area and volume to real modeling problems. The course closes with the CA Geometry conditional probability standards. Compass, straightedge, patty paper and free dynamic geometry software (GeoGebra) are used throughout.

courses.title: Chemistry in the Earth System
courses.description: The second course in California's three-course NGSS high school model, connecting chemistry to Earth's systems. Students investigate combustion, atomic structure and the origin of elements in stars, bonding and material properties, energy flow in the Earth system, reaction stoichiometry, the chemistry of climate change, reaction rates and equilibrium, and ocean acidification. Every week includes a hands-on investigation with household materials or a PhET simulation, plus data analysis and claim-evidence-reasoning writing.

courses.title: Modern World History
courses.description: Grade 10 World History, Culture, and Geography: The Modern World, following CA HSS standards 10.1–10.11. Students trace the ideas of democracy from Athens and the Enlightenment through the Atlantic revolutions, industrialization, imperialism, two world wars, totalitarian regimes, the Cold War, decolonization, and globalization. Each week centers on primary sources (documents, speeches, photographs, maps) analyzed with sourcing and corroboration, building toward document-based essays and a research project.
courses.framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards (Grade 10); 2016 CA History–Social Science Framework

standards.10.1: Relate the moral and ethical principles in ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, Judaism, and Christianity to the development of Western political thought.
standards.10.1.1: Analyze similarities and differences in Judeo-Christian and Greco-Roman views of law, reason and faith, and duties of the individual.
standards.10.1.2: Trace the development of the Western political ideas of the rule of law and illegitimacy of tyranny, using Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Politics.
standards.10.1.3: Consider the influence of the U.S. Constitution on political systems in the contemporary world.
standards.10.2: Compare and contrast the Glorious Revolution of England, the American Revolution, and the French Revolution and their enduring effects worldwide.
standards.10.2.1: Compare the major ideas of philosophers (Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Jefferson, Madison) and their effects on democratic revolutions.
standards.10.2.2: List the principles of the Magna Carta, English Bill of Rights, Declaration of Independence, and Declaration of the Rights of Man.
standards.10.2.3: Understand the unique character of the American Revolution, its spread to Latin America, and its effect on the French Revolution.
standards.10.2.4: Explain how the ideology of the French Revolution led France to develop from constitutional monarchy to democratic despotism to the Napoleonic empire.
standards.10.2.5: Discuss how nationalism spread across Europe with Napoleon but was repressed for a generation under the Congress of Vienna.
standards.10.3: Analyze the effects of the Industrial Revolution in England, France, Germany, Japan, and the United States.
standards.10.3.1: Analyze why England was the first country to industrialize.
standards.10.3.2: Examine how scientific and technological changes and new forms of energy brought about economic and social change.
standards.10.3.3: Describe the growth of population, rural to urban migration, and growth of cities.
standards.10.3.4: Trace the evolution of work and labor, including slavery's demise, child labor, unions, and the role of women.
standards.10.3.5: Understand the connections among natural resources, entrepreneurship, labor, and capital.
standards.10.3.6: Analyze the emergence of capitalism and responses to it, including utopianism, socialism, and communism.
standards.10.3.7: Describe the emergence of Romanticism in art and literature and social criticism by writers such as Dickens.
standards.10.4: Analyze patterns of global change in the era of New Imperialism in at least two regions (Africa, Southeast Asia, China, India, Latin America, Philippines).

courses.title: Spanish III
courses.description: Spanish III moves students from Novice High toward Intermediate Mid proficiency through themed units on identity, childhood memories, travel, health, the environment, art and literature, community and work, technology, and celebrations across the Spanish-speaking world. Grammar focuses on preterite vs. imperfect, commands, the future and conditional, perfect tenses, and the present and imperfect subjunctive. Each week balances interpretive reading/listening with authentic sources, interpersonal conversation, presentational speaking and writing, and cultural comparison.

courses.title: Music & Media Arts
courses.description: A year-long arts course that combines music literacy and creation with digital media arts. Semester 1 builds notation, rhythm, harmony, songwriting and critical listening across world and American music traditions, ending in a recorded showcase. Semester 2 applies those skills to media arts: photography and design, audio production and podcasting, video editing and film scoring, culminating in an original multimedia capstone. All production uses free browser tools (BandLab, Chrome Music Lab, Audacity, free video editors).

courses.title: PE 10 (Course 2)
courses.description: High School Physical Education Course 2, following the CA model content standards for adventure/outdoor activities, combatives (self-defense), individual and dual activities, dance, aquatics/gymnastics, and team activities. Students take the Physical Fitness Test (FITNESSGRAM) items, design and monitor personal fitness plans using FITT principles, and study the psychological and social aspects of activity such as leadership, group dynamics, and risk management. Activities are adapted for home, parks, and community facilities.
courses.framework: California Physical Education Model Content Standards (High School Course 2); 2009 CA Physical Education Framework

standards.PE-HS2-1.1: Demonstrate proficient movement skills in outdoor/adventure activities (e.g., hiking, orienteering, climbing).
standards.PE-HS2-1.2: Explain and apply safety practices and risk management in adventure and outdoor activities.
standards.PE-HS2-1.3: Demonstrate basic self-defense and combative skills, including escapes, falls and blocks.

standards.PE-HS2-1.6: Demonstrate proficient skills in dance and rhythmic activities, including creating a movement sequence.
standards.PE-HS2-1.7: Demonstrate proficient skills in gymnastics/tumbling or aquatics activities with correct technique and safety.
standards.PE-HS2-1.8: Demonstrate advanced offensive, defensive, and transition strategies in team activities.
standards.PE-HS2-1.9: Apply biomechanical principles (force, leverage, levers, center of gravity) to analyze and improve performance.
standards.PE-HS2-2.1: Participate in moderate to vigorous physical activity at least four days each week.
standards.PE-HS2-2.2: Meet health-fitness standards for aerobic capacity, body composition, muscular strength, endurance, and flexibility (FITNESSGRAM).
standards.PE-HS2-2.3: Develop and implement a personal fitness plan using the FITT principles and monitor progress.
standards.PE-HS2-2.4: Explain the relationship between nutrition, hydration, rest, and performance.
standards.PE-HS2-2.5: Use heart-rate monitoring and perceived exertion to regulate training intensity.
standards.PE-HS2-3.1: Explain and demonstrate leadership, cooperation and group dynamics in physical activity settings.
standards.PE-HS2-3.2: Accept responsibility for personal safety and the safety of others; demonstrate ethical behavior and sportsmanship.
standards.PE-HS2-3.3: Identify and evaluate the benefits of lifelong participation in physical activity, including community resources.

courses.subject: HEALTH
courses.title: Driver Education (S1) & First Aid/CPR + Health II (S2)
courses.description: Semester 1 is a classroom Driver Education course built on the California DMV Driver Handbook, covering the topics required before a minor may apply for an instruction permit at 15½: licensing and the provisional (GDL) rules, vehicle controls, signs and pavement markings, right-of-way, speed laws, lane use and parking, freeway driving, sharing the road, hazardous conditions, impaired and distracted driving, and collisions and insurance; it ends with full-length practice knowledge tests. Semester 2 combines First Aid, CPR and AED skills with Health II topics: mental and emotional health, substance use prevention (including fentanyl awareness), nutrition and consumer health, healthy relationships, and community and environmental health.
courses.framework: California DMV Driver Handbook (current edition) and CA Education Code driver-education requirements; 2008 California Health Education Content Standards (Grades 9–12); 2019 CA Health Education Framework

standards.DE-1: Licensing: instruction permit requirements (age 15½, driver ed, knowledge and vision tests), provisional license rules (6-month permit, 50 supervised hours incl. 10 at night, passenger and 11 p.m.–5 a.m. restrictions), and license classes.
standards.DE-2: Vehicle readiness: controls, instruments, pre-drive checks, seat/mirror adjustment, seat belts, airbags, and child passenger restraints.
standards.DE-3: Traffic signs (shapes and colors), traffic signals, and pavement markings and lane lines; curb colors.
standards.DE-4: Right-of-way rules at intersections, roundabouts, crosswalks, and for pedestrians and emergency vehicles.
standards.DE-5: Turning, signaling, lane changes, passing, U-turns, lane positioning, and parking (including hills and parallel parking).
standards.DE-6: Speed laws: the Basic Speed Law, maximum and posted limits, school and residential zones, and following distance.
standards.DE-7: Sharing the road with pedestrians, bicyclists (3-foot rule), motorcyclists, large trucks, buses, light rail, and slow-moving vehicles.
standards.DE-8: Freeway driving: entering, merging, exiting, carpool/HOV lanes, and interchanges.
standards.DE-9: Hazardous conditions and defensive driving: night, rain, fog, wind, smoke, skids, space cushions, scanning, and the Move Over law.
standards.DE-10: Alcohol and drugs: effects on driving, BAC limits (0.08 adults; 0.01 under 21), implied consent, open-container and DUI penalties.
standards.DE-11: Distracted and drowsy driving: California cell-phone laws (minors may not use any wireless device), and fatigue management.
standards.DE-12: Collisions and emergencies: what to do after a collision, reporting (SR-1), insurance and financial responsibility, vehicle emergencies, and the point count system.
standards.DE-13: Railroad crossings, school buses, work zones, and special road situations.
standards.DE-14: Preparation for the DMV knowledge test: test-taking strategies and full practice examinations.
standards.H-HS.1.1.S: Describe ways to reduce the risk of injuries as a driver or passenger, including seat belt use and avoiding impaired driving.
standards.H-HS.1.4.S: Explain the relationship between substance use, distraction, and fatigue and the risk of motor-vehicle injuries.
standards.H-HS.1.9.S: Describe the procedures for basic first aid, CPR, choking, and use of an AED.
standards.H-HS.5.1.S: Use a decision-making process to evaluate risky situations, such as riding with an impaired or distracted driver.
standards.H-HS.7.2.S: Demonstrate basic first aid and CPR/AED procedures.
standards.H-HS.8.1.S: Encourage others to adopt safe behaviors, including safe driving practices.
standards.H-HS.1.2.M: Describe the signs, symptoms, and treatment of common mental health conditions, including depression and anxiety.
standards.H-HS.1.5.M: Identify warning signs of suicide and appropriate ways to seek help for self and others.
standards.H-HS.3.1.M: Identify trusted adults and community resources (including 988) for mental health support.
standards.H-HS.7.1.M: Practice stress management and coping strategies.
standards.H-HS.4.1.M: Use effective communication and conflict-resolution skills.
standards.H-HS.1.2.A: Explain the short- and long-term effects of alcohol, cannabis, nicotine/vaping, and other drugs, including fentanyl.
standards.H-HS.2.1.A: Analyze influences such as media, peers, and advertising on substance use.
standards.H-HS.4.2.A: Demonstrate refusal and negotiation skills to avoid substance use.
standards.H-HS.3.2.A: Locate valid information and services for substance use prevention and treatment, including naloxone access.
standards.H-HS.1.1.N: Explain the relationship between nutrition, physical activity, and health, and interpret food labels.
standards.H-HS.6.1.N: Develop a personal plan for healthy eating and physical activity.
standards.H-HS.2.1.P: Evaluate health products, services, and advertising claims as an informed consumer.
standards.H-HS.1.6.P: Explain how environmental factors such as air quality and water affect personal and community health.
standards.H-HS.1.3.G: Describe characteristics of healthy and unhealthy relationships, consent, and how to prevent dating violence.
standards.H-HS.1.6.G: Explain how to access reproductive and sexual health services and accurate information (CA Healthy Youth Act).

courses.title: Computer Science Principles
courses.description: A full-year introductory computer science course modeled on the AP Computer Science Principles framework and taught primarily with Code.org's free CSP curriculum. Students study how digital information is represented, how the internet works, event-driven app design, programming with variables, conditionals, lists, loops and procedures, algorithms and efficiency, data analysis and simulation, cybersecurity and cryptography, and the social impacts of computing, with a short bridge to Python. The year ends with an AP-style Create Performance Task and exam review; homeschool students can register for the May AP CSP exam through a local host school. Graded as a college-preparatory elective (UC/CSU 'g'); a UC-approved online provider is needed for a home-designed course to appear on a UC transcript.

units.title: Digital Information
units.big_idea: Everything a computer stores—numbers, text, images, sound—is an abstraction built from bits.

units.title: The Internet
units.big_idea: The internet works because of open protocols, redundancy and layers of abstraction, not a single central computer.

units.title: Intro to App Design and Programming
units.big_idea: Programs are built iteratively: design for users, write event-driven code, test and debug.

units.title: Variables, Lists, Loops and Traversals
units.big_idea: Collections and iteration let one short program process any amount of data.

units.title: Functions, Libraries and Algorithms
units.big_idea: Abstraction through procedures and libraries manages complexity; algorithms differ in efficiency and some problems cannot be solved.

units.title: Data and Simulation
units.big_idea: Data can reveal patterns and inform decisions, but how it is collected and modeled can introduce bias.

units.title: Cybersecurity and Global Impacts
units.big_idea: Computing innovations create benefits and harms; encryption and safe practices protect people's data.

days.work: Use App Lab's data library to load a real dataset into lists.

days.title: Check
days.work: Solve six traversal problems (count matches, find max, average, filter by length, map to uppercase, find first index) in App Lab.

weeks.topic: Data app project and semester exam
objectives: Build an app that processes real data

days.title: Plan
days.work: Choose a dataset from the App Lab data library and plan an app that filters it based on user input.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the data app so a dropdown choice filters the dataset with a traversal and displays matching results and a count.

days.title: Test
days.work: Have a user try three different inputs, record any wrong or empty results, and refine the app to handle them.

days.title: Semester review
days.work: Review units 1–4 by completing 30 AP-style practice questions and making a one-page summary sheet of missed concepts.

days.title: Semester exam
days.work: Take the semester exam: 50 AP-style multiple-choice questions covering data, the internet and programming through traversals.

weeks.topic: Procedures with parameters and return values

days.title: Procedures
days.work: Find repeated code in an earlier app and refactor it into a named procedure, confirming the app behaves identically.

days.title: Parameters
days.work: Write procedures with parameters for drawing shapes of different sizes.

days.title: Return values
days.work: Write functions that return values (tip calculator, letter grade, area of a circle) and use the returned values in expressions.

days.title: Decomposition
days.work: Decompose a game into procedures on a diagram before coding.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete 10 AP-style questions tracing PROCEDURE calls with parameters and RETURN values.

days.title: Libraries
days.work: Read App Lab library documentation and use a library function.

days.title: Create a library
days.work: Write your own library of three functions with documentation.

days.title: Share
days.work: Share your library and use a partner's or a Code.org example library.

days.title: Licensing
days.work: Research the license of a popular open-source library (e.g., p5.js) and explain usage limits.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a documentation comment (purpose, parameters, return value, example) for each function in your library and take a short quiz.

days.title: Linear search
days.work: Search for a target card in a shuffled deck of 52 cards one at a time, counting steps over five trials.

days.title: Binary search
days.work: Search a sorted deck using binary search and compare the steps.

days.title: Efficiency
days.work: Graph worst-case steps vs. list size (8 to 1,024) for linear and binary search and describe the growth as linear vs. logarithmic.

days.title: Across disciplines
days.work: Show how binary search applies to a dictionary, debugging and guessing games.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete AP-style questions classifying algorithms as reasonable (polynomial) or unreasonable (exponential) time.

weeks.topic: Unsolvable problems, heuristics and parallel computing
objectives: Compare sequential, parallel and distributed computing

days.title: Traveling salesperson
days.work: Try to find the shortest route through 6 cities and count the possibilities.

days.title: Heuristics
days.work: Use a nearest-neighbor heuristic and compare to the best route.

days.title: Undecidable problems
days.work: Read about Turing's halting problem and write a paragraph explaining in your own words why no program can decide whether every program halts.

days.title: Parallel computing
days.work: Time sorting cards alone vs. with helpers and calculate speedup.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take the Unit 5 assessment on procedures, libraries, search algorithms, efficiency and parallel computing.

days.title: Data questions
days.work: Write a question to investigate (e.g., teen sleep vs. screen time) and design a 6-question survey with consistent answer formats.

days.title: Collect
days.work: Collect survey responses from at least 15 people using Google Forms and export them to a spreadsheet.

days.title: Clean
days.work: Clean the data by standardizing entries and removing duplicates.

days.title: Storage tradeoffs
days.work: Compare storing data in a spreadsheet vs. a database vs. cloud storage.

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit the cleaned dataset with a reflection on what cleaning decisions you made and how they could affect conclusions.

objectives: Choose an appropriate chart type for a question

days.title: Chart types
days.work: Compare bar, line, scatter and histogram charts using four sample datasets and write which question each chart answers best.

days.title: Pivot tables
days.work: Build a pivot table in Google Sheets that summarizes your survey responses by category and counts or averages each group.

days.title: Visualize your data
days.work: Create three different charts from your cleaned survey data, each with a clear title, labeled axes and a one-sentence takeaway.

days.title: Large public data
days.work: Download a CA dataset (e.g., daily temperatures or AQI from a public source) and make a line chart showing a trend over time, noting outliers.

days.title: Check
days.work: Present a 3-slide data story (question, visualization, conclusion and limitations) to a parent and answer two follow-up questions.

weeks.assessment: Data story presentation scored with rubric.

objectives: Build a simulation using random numbers
Refine a model so it better matches real data

days.title: Why simulate?
days.work: Read the Code.org simulations lesson and list three real simulations (weather, traffic, epidemics) and what each simplifies.

days.title: Random numbers
days.work: Write an App Lab program that flips a coin 1,000 times with randomNumber(0,1) and compare the result to the expected 50%.

days.title: Build a model
days.work: Build a checkout-line simulation where customers arrive randomly and one cashier serves them; record the average wait.

days.title: Refine the model
days.work: Time real arrivals at a store or drive-through for 15 minutes, then change your model's arrival rate and add a second cashier to match.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining what your model leaves out, how refinement changed its predictions, and one decision it could inform.

weeks.topic: Bias in data and machine learning
objectives: Identify sources of bias in data and algorithms
Propose processes to evaluate and reduce bias

days.title: Bias in data
days.work: Identify the sampling bias in five survey scenarios (e.g., an online-only poll about internet access) and rewrite one to fix it.

days.title: Machine learning
days.work: Train an image classifier in Teachable Machine with deliberately unbalanced training data, then retrain with balanced data and compare accuracy.

days.title: Algorithmic bias
days.work: Read a credible news article on facial recognition or hiring-algorithm bias and identify where in the pipeline the bias entered.

days.title: Crowdsourcing and fixes
days.work: Explore a citizen-science project (e.g., Zooniverse) and write a checklist developers can use to test an app for bias.

days.title: Unit 6 test
days.work: Take the Unit 6 assessment on data collection, visualization, simulation and bias.

objectives: Evaluate the tradeoffs of automated data collection

days.title: PII inventory
days.work: List the personally identifiable information you have shared with apps and websites and rate the risk of each item.

days.title: Tracking
days.work: Inspect cookies and site permissions in your browser, then use a tracker-visualizer extension or privacy report to count third-party trackers on a news site.

days.title: Privacy policies
days.work: Read the privacy policy of an app you use and summarize what data it collects, who it shares with, and how to delete it.

days.title: California privacy law
days.work: Learn the rights the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) gives residents and draft a data-deletion request email.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a 400-word argument on whether location tracking for safety is worth the privacy cost, using evidence from this week.

objectives: Encrypt and decrypt with symmetric ciphers
Explain how public key encryption enables secure communication

days.title: Caesar cipher
days.work: Encrypt a sentence with a Caesar cipher, then crack a partner's message by trying all 25 shifts with the Code.org widget.

days.title: Frequency analysis
days.work: Use the Code.org frequency-analysis widget to crack a random-substitution cipher and explain why letter frequencies leak information.

days.title: Vigenère cipher
days.work: Encrypt with a Vigenère cipher using a keyword and explain why a longer key is harder to crack.

days.title: Public key
days.work: Model public key exchange with the paint-mixing analogy, then explain how HTTPS uses public keys when you load a website.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a cryptography quiz comparing symmetric and asymmetric encryption and computationally hard problems.

objectives: Compare security measures for different threats

days.title: Threat research
days.work: Research phishing, malware, ransomware and DDoS attacks and make a chart of how each works and a real example.

days.title: Spot the phish
days.work: Analyze 10 sample emails and texts, label each as legitimate or phishing, and list the clues.

days.title: Passwords and MFA
days.work: Calculate the number of possible passwords for 8 vs. 16 characters and turn on multifactor authentication for one of your accounts.

days.title: Security measures
days.work: Match firewalls, antivirus, encryption, software updates and backups to the threats they address and note their limits.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a one-page cybersecurity guide for your family with five specific actions and why each matters.

objectives: Research a computing innovation's beneficial and harmful effects
Use credible sources to support claims

days.title: Choose an innovation
days.work: Pick a computing innovation (generative AI, self-driving cars, facial recognition, ride-sharing apps) and write three research questions.

days.title: Research
days.work: Find at least three credible sources and record evidence on data used, benefits, harms and who is affected.

days.title: Effects analysis
days.work: Build a table of intended vs. unintended and beneficial vs. harmful effects on social, economic and cultural life.

days.title: Write
days.work: Write a 600-word impact essay with citations taking a position on how the innovation should be used or regulated.

days.title: Unit 7 test
days.work: Take the Unit 7 assessment on privacy, cryptography, cybersecurity and impacts.

objectives: Write Python programs with variables, input, conditionals and loops

days.title: Hello, Python
days.work: Create a Trinket account, write print statements, and fix three syntax errors in a provided program.

days.title: Variables and input
days.work: Write a Python tip calculator using input(), float() conversion and formatted output.

days.title: Conditionals
days.work: Rewrite your App Lab pet-quiz logic in Python using if/elif/else and compare the two versions side by side.

days.title: Loops
days.work: Write a number-guessing game with a while loop and a times-table printer with a for loop and range().

days.title: Check
days.work: Solve five short Python practice problems (even/odd, FizzBuzz, sum to n, grade letter, countdown) and submit them.

objectives: Use lists and functions in Python

days.title: Lists
days.work: Create Python lists, use append, len and slicing, and traverse a list of test scores to find the max and average.

days.title: Functions
days.work: Write functions with parameters and return values (e.g., to_fahrenheit, is_vowel) and test each with three inputs.

days.title: CS50 lecture
days.work: Watch the CS50 Python-week lecture segment on functions and lists and note two ideas that match what you did in App Lab.

days.title: Mini project
days.work: Build a Python program (gradebook, quiz game or word counter) that uses a list, a loop and at least two functions in a separate module.

days.title: Check
days.work: Demonstrate the mini project and explain how your functions decompose the problem.

objectives: Plan a program meeting the AP Create task requirements

days.title: Requirements
days.work: Read the College Board Create task requirements and make a checklist: input, list, procedure with parameter, sequencing/selection/iteration, output.

days.title: Brainstorm
days.work: Brainstorm five program ideas for a real user and score each on purpose, feasibility and how naturally it uses a list.

days.title: Plan
days.work: Write a program plan with the purpose, the list and what it manages, and the student-developed procedure and its algorithm in pseudocode.

days.title: Prototype
days.work: Sketch the user interface screens and walk a potential user through them to collect feedback.

days.title: Check
days.work: Review the plan against the checklist with a parent and revise any missing requirement.

days.title: Interface
days.work: Build the program's screens and event handlers in App Lab (or Python) and log your progress.

days.title: List
days.work: Code the list that stores your program's data and display it to verify it is populated correctly.

days.title: Procedure
days.work: Write the student-developed procedure with a parameter that uses sequencing, selection and iteration.

days.title: Test
days.work: Write and run at least four test cases, including edge cases, recording expected vs. actual results.

days.title: Peer review
days.work: Share your program with a CS peer through an online community or co-op and give/receive feedback using a collaborative document.

weeks.topic: Create Performance Task: refine and document
objectives: Refine the program using user feedback
Record the video and complete the Personalized Project Reference

days.title: User testing
days.work: Have two users test the program, note usability and accessibility problems, and prioritize fixes.

days.title: Refine
days.work: Fix the top issues, add code comments, and acknowledge any code or media from others with correct license attribution.

days.title: Video
days.work: Record a 1-minute-or-less screen video showing input, program functionality and output.

days.title: Written responses
days.work: Capture your list and procedure code segments in a Personalized Project Reference and practice the written-response prompts about them.

days.title: Submit
days.work: Submit the program code, video and PPR, and self-score with the College Board rubric.

weeks.assessment: Create task self-score with the AP rubric.

objectives: Review all five AP CSP big ideas
Demonstrate mastery on a cumulative exam

days.title: Review: data and networks
days.work: Complete Khan Academy AP CSP practice on binary, compression, the internet and fault tolerance and correct every error.

days.title: Review: programming
days.work: Trace 20 AP reference-sheet pseudocode problems on lists, loops, procedures and Boolean logic.

days.title: Practice exam
days.work: Take a timed 70-question AP-style practice exam under test conditions (120 minutes).

days.title: Error analysis
days.work: Categorize missed practice-exam questions by big idea and redo each with a written explanation.

days.title: Final exam
days.work: Take the cumulative course final and write a short reflection on your growth as a programmer.
